Hussin Fekry · Dr. Ahmed S. Dalaq

Sutures: the shape that holds two parts together.

A suture is a wavy, interlocking seam between two stiff parts. Nature uses it in skull bones, ammonite shells, turtle shells and the woodpecker beak. When you pull the parts apart, the hooks of the seam push against each other, so the shape of the line decides how strong and how tough the joint is.

This project designs such seams on a computer: a few points and a smooth curve make one suture, a simulation pulls it apart, and an AI model learns which shapes hold best.

a few points→smooth curve→is it a real hook?→pull-out simulation→AI learns the strength
Shape
Same material, different line: the geometry alone changes the strength.
Points
Two fixed ends and a few free points, joined in an order, describe one suture.
Pull
The left part is held, the right part is pulled; the force tells us how good the hook is.
Learn
A neural network reads the suture image and predicts its strength in a moment.

01 · Design lab

Drag the free points. The checks run live.

Each free point may move inside its dashed box (|δx| ≤ 0.45 L, 0.5 mm from the walls). The curve is the same PCHIP spline and the same checks as suture_geometry.py, rewritten in JavaScript and tested against the Python code on 17,505 designs.

Control points N
Path: the order the curve visits the points ()

    Nearest design we simulated

    The curve is the Abaqus pull-out test of that design: the right part is pulled to the right by u (x axis) and the line shows the force needed (y axis). The force rises while the hook resists, reaches the peak force (strength), and falls when the hook slides out. Steep start = stiff; area under the curve = energy (toughness). Picked by: same N and path, closest free points. It is a real result for a nearby design, not a prediction for yours.

    02 · Path gallery

    Same points, every order.

    The free points of the design lab stay where they are; only the visiting order changes. With N − 2 free points there are (N − 2)! paths, because each free point is visited exactly once and the two ends are fixed. Click a card to load that path.

    03 · Design space

    How many sutures are there?

    On a 9-level grid each free point has 9 × 9 = 81 places. The total is 81N−2 × (N − 2)!. For N = 4 every design was checked; for N = 5 and 6 the class shares are estimated from 30,000 random grid designs each.

    04 · Universe

    Every dot is one whole suture.

    Horizontal position: mean δx/L and mean δy/L of the free points. Height inside each layer: curve length (short at the bottom, long and hooked at the top). Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, click a dot to see its suture. A small jitter (±0.025) keeps equal means apart.

    Small dots = grid designs, only their shape was checked; colour = shape class:

    Big dots = designs simulated in Abaqus; colour = peak force:

    05 · Abaqus pull-out

    396 real force–displacement curves.

    The left part is held and the right part is pulled (2D plane stress, frictional contact). Each line is one design, coloured by its peak force. Hover to find a design. Shown: first-solver-attempt runs of the 2 Nov table; re-runs by the old solver are left out because they were biased.

    1 N

    Hovered design

    Move over the curves.

    Model check: jigsaw cell vs analytical model (Malik et al. 2017)

    Peak traction 2.313 vs 2.376 MPa (−2.7%); RMS error 3.0% of the peak. This checks the contact model against the analytical model, not against a physical test.

    06 · CNN surrogate

    From the suture image to peak force, stiffness and toughness.

    A CNN reads the 128 × 128 suture image (no other input) and predicts the three properties. Median relative error on load-bearing N = 4 test designs, test set opened once (12 Nov). 5-fold grouped cross-validation gives the larger-sample estimate.

    N = 4 test set (45 designs, 28 twin groups)

    Peak force error by model

    Cross-validation (N = 4, 489 designs)

    Other N (CNN, peak force, cross-validation): N = 5 6.5%, N = 6 11.7%. Mirror-twin noise floor of the FE data: 0.2% median.
